:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: Consider the vector field $\mathbf{F}=(2x-y)^2\,\mathbf{i}+(3y-2z)^2\,\mathbf{j}+(x-2z)^2\,\mathbf{k}.$ Evaluate $\textrm{div}\,\mathbf{F}$ at the point $(1,2,1).$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
If $\mathbf{F}=P\,\mathbf{i}+Q\,\mathbf{j} + R\,\mathbf k$ is a vector field on $\mathbb{R}^3$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $\mathbf F$ all exist, then the divergence of $\mathbf F$ is the scalar field given by

$$
\textrm{div}\,\mathbf F = \nabla\cdot\mathbf{F}=\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x}+\dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y}+\dfrac{\partial R}{\partial z}.
$$

  

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\cdot F & =\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}+\frac{∂R}{∂z} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}((2x-y)^{2})+\frac{∂}{∂y}((3y-2z)^{2})+\frac{∂}{∂z}((x-2z)^{2}) \\  & =4(2x-y)+6(3y-2z)-4(x-2z) \\  & =4x+14y-4z.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate $\textrm{div}\,\mathbf { F}$ at the point $(1,2,1),$ and obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{div}\,F(1,2,1) & =4(1)+14(2)-4(1) \\  & =28.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
∇\cdot F=\text{div}\,F=\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}+\frac{∂R}{∂z}.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\cdot F & =\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}+\frac{∂R}{∂z} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy))+\frac{∂}{∂y}(-y\operatorname{cos}⁡x)+\frac{∂}{∂z}(y{z}^{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{x}-\operatorname{cos}⁡x+3y{z}^{2}.\end{aligned}

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: Consider the vector field $F=(x-y)^{3}\,i+(y+z)^{3}\,j+(x+z)^{3}\,k.$ Evaluate $\text{div}\,F$ at the point $(-2,2,2).$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j+R\,k$ is a vector field on ${R}^{3}$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $F$ all exist, then the divergence of $F$ is the scalar field given by

$$
\text{div}\,F=∇\cdot F=\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}+\frac{∂R}{∂z}.
$$

  

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\cdot F & =\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}+\frac{∂R}{∂z} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}((x-y)^{3})+\frac{∂}{∂y}((y+z)^{3})+\frac{∂}{∂z}((x+z)^{3}) \\  & =3(x-y)^{2}+3(y+z)^{2}+3(x+z)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we evaluate $\text{div}\,F$ at the point $(-2,2,2),$ and obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{div}\,F(-2,2,2) & =3((-2)-(2))^{2}+3((2)+(2))^{2}+3((-2)+(2))^{2} \\  & =3(-4)^{2}+3(4)^{2}+3(0)^{2} \\  & =96.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}(∇\cdot F)(1,1,0) & =1\cdot {e}^{0}+\operatorname{ln}⁡1+1\cdot {e}^{0}+1+1 \\  & =1+0+1+1+1 \\  & =4.\end{aligned}

$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: Consider the vector field $F={x}^{2}yz\,i+{x}^{3}y\,j+z\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{y}{x})\,k.$ Evaluate $\text{div}\,F$ at the point $(-1,-1,2).$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j+R\,k$ is a vector field on ${R}^{3}$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $F$ all exist, then the divergence of $F$ is the scalar field given by

$$
\text{div}\,F=∇\cdot F=\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}+\frac{∂R}{∂z}.
$$

  

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\cdot F & =\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}+\frac{∂R}{∂z} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}yz)+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{3}y)+\frac{∂}{∂z}(z\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{y}{x})) \\  & =2xyz+{x}^{3}+\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{y}{x})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate $\text{div}\,F$ at the point $(-1,-1,2),$ and obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{div}\,F(-1,-1,2) & =2(-1)(-1)(2)+(-1)^{3}+\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{-1}{-1}) \\  & =4-1+\frac{\pi }{4} \\  & =3+\frac{\pi }{4}.\end{aligned}
$$
